**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I sit here, staring at the blank page, the cursor blinking like a metronome counting down the seconds of my life. A thousand words. It sounds like a lot, but words are slippery things—sometimes they spill out in a rush, and other times they cling to the edges of my mind, refusing to be pinned down.

I think about the weight of words. How some can lift you up, while others drag you under. A single sentence can change a life, for better or worse. "I love you." "You’re fired." "It’s over." Three words, each carrying the force of a storm. And yet, here I am, tasked with filling a thousand of them, as if quantity alone could measure meaning.

The world outside my window is quiet. The trees sway gently, their leaves whispering secrets to the wind. I wonder if they know how lucky they are—existing without the burden of language. They don’t have to explain themselves. They don’t have to justify their growth or apologize for their shadows. They simply *are*.

But humans? We’re tangled in words. We build lives with them, tear them down, stitch them back together. We argue over definitions, twist meanings, and hide behind silence when words fail us. And yet, we keep trying. We keep speaking, writing, shouting into the void, hoping someone—anyone—will hear us.

I remember the first time I realized words had power. I was eight years old, and my teacher told me my story was "beautiful." Just one word, but it lit something inside me. For the first time, I felt seen. And then, years later, when someone called me "worthless," that word burrowed into my bones and stayed there, a ghost I couldn’t shake.

Words are alive. They breathe, they evolve, they die. Some words are relics of a time we’ve outgrown, while others are born from necessity, filling gaps we didn’t know existed. "Selfie." "Unfriend." "Gaslighting." Words that didn’t exist a generation ago now shape how we see the world.

And what about the words we don’t say? The ones that sit heavy on our tongues, unsaid out of fear or shame or love? The "I’m sorry" we swallow, the "I need help" we bury, the "I miss you" we type and delete. Those words have weight too. Maybe more than the ones we let loose.

I wonder if the trees ever feel this way—if they ever wish they could speak, or if they’re glad they don’t have to. Maybe silence is its own kind of language. Maybe the spaces between words are just as important as the words themselves.

A thousand words. I’ve used a fraction of them, and already, I feel the pull of the unsaid. There’s so much more I could write—the way sunlight looks at 3 PM, the smell of rain on hot pavement, the ache of a memory that won’t fade. But words can only do so much. They can point at the truth, but they can’t always hold it.

So I’ll stop here, with the cursor still blinking, the page still half-empty. Maybe the rest is for you to fill in. Maybe the real magic isn’t in the words I’ve written, but in the ones you’ll think of after reading them.

After all, a thousand words is just the beginning. The rest is silence. The rest is yours.
